topic: The Windmill Problem (Computational Geometry & Rotational Invariants)
target_audience: Advanced high school students or undergraduate math students

sections.title: Problem Introduction: The Spinning Line
sections.content: Define the setup: n points on a 2D plane with a line passing through one of them. The line rotates until it hits another point, then pivots around that new point, continuing the rotation. Goal: Prove the line eventually hits every point infinitely.
sections.example: Visualize 5 ladybugs on a leaf; a 'laser beam' pivots on the ladybugs, sweeping across the leaf like a radar.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Angles and Slopes
sections.content: Establish that the total angle rotated is the invariant. Explain how the direction of the line changes as it hits a point: the rotation angle is always positive (counter-clockwise).
sections.example: A clock hand moving past numbers; explain that 'jumping' from one pivot to the next is equivalent to adding the angle between the two lines.

sections.title: The Core Mechanism: The Pivot Rule
sections.content: Illustrate the geometry: when the line hits a point 'B' while pivoting on 'A', the line effectively rotates by an angle theta to become the line pivoting on 'B'. Use an animation of the line 'snapping' to the next available point.
sections.example: A bicycle gear shifting: the chain (the line) moves from one tooth (point) to the next as the wheel rotates.

sections.title: The Invariant Principle
sections.content: Explain the key proof concept: Since the total angle rotated is finite in one full 180-degree sweep, and the rotation is unidirectional, the line must visit every point to maintain the 'conservation of rotation'.
sections.example: A lighthouse rotating; if the lighthouse hits every sector of the ocean, it must encounter every island (point) in its path.

sections.title: Synthesis & Summary
sections.content: Summarize that the Windmill Problem is a classic example of using 'invariants' to solve dynamic geometry problems. Encourage students to visualize the sweep as a continuous angular accumulation.
sections.example: A recap animation showing the line completing one full rotation (180 degrees) and proving it has 'exhausted' all points as potential pivots.
